findings.text: The terminal glue for this virtual console exposes attach points for session establishment, session start, session end, resource release, line drop, output transfer, output capacity query, pending output query and input flow signals. An implementation provides these hooks through the terminal operations vector.

Device selection is by numeric position within a global registry. Installation fails when no entry matches, otherwise it guarantees partner reachability before binding, clears any prior staged output, associates terminal and device records mutually, records a pending inbound poll, and finalizes enablement outside the device guard. Failure during enablement or port linkage unwinds with interrupt suppression and reference release.

Session accounting uses a per-device usage count with mutual terminal linkage. Start increments the count and requests inbound processing plus a background wake. Normal end decrements and, on reaching zero, detaches the terminal, suppresses interrupts, waits briefly for drain, then releases the interrupt line. Cleanup clears the linkage and drops a reference. Line drop discards scheduled work, buffered bytes and count state while also suppressing interrupts and releasing the line. Hung-up handles and missing linkage close as no-ops, and a negative count indicates misuse.

Output is staged through a fixed per-device buffer with upper truncation of oversized caller requests. Accepted bytes are counted as delivered once staged, with an immediate attempt to hand the staging area to the hypervisor unless a background retry is already pending. Lack of space stops acceptance, a negative transfer result is reported as an input output failure, and capacity queries report free versus occupied staging space with zero room when unbound or idle.

A global registry guard nests outside each per-device guard. Registry traversal holds the outer guard while briefly acquiring the inner guard per entry for comparison. Device state, usage count, linkage, staging counts and work flags are mutated only under the inner guard with interrupt state preserved. Operations that may sleep, such as device enablement and drain wait, run outside guards, snapshotting needed identifiers beforehand.

Load registers the virtual bus driver and reports success. Unload unregisters that driver, stops the background helper when present, releases a shared information page under its dedicated guard, unregisters the terminal driver, clears the index allocation list and drops the driver reference.
The hypervisor console uses major 229 with base minor 128 and supports at most four ports.
Protocol version is one. Largest packet is 256 bytes, largest single inbound chunk is 16 bytes, largest outbound payload fragment is 12 bytes, and small outbound accounting holds 12 bytes.
State waits use five times the tick rate. Per-packet terminal delivery is capped at 128 bytes.

Per-port state aggregates a terminal port anchor, deferred output and handshake work items, two wait queues for output empty and protocol phase change, a guard, a numeric index, three byte areas for surplus deferral and small outbound accounting and larger inbound reassembly with an end marker, surplus and outbound counts, terminal and interrupt identifiers, a monotonic packet counter, modem bits, a protocol phase byte, option flags with one bit marking console use, and an optional attention marker when that feature is compiled. Version responses and queries require long alignment.

Ports live in a fixed array sized by the maximum port count, with a global driver anchor, a live count, and a pluggable phase waiter invoked with a port and a desired phase. Early bring-up uses polling while later operation uses sleeping waits.

The link phase can be idle closed, expecting a version answer, expecting a version inquiry, established, expecting modem status, or peer failed. Established includes the modem wait as already usable. Console marking is a separate flag test. Phase updates always notify all phase waiters, with one helper assuming the port guard is held and another acquiring it with interrupt preservation. A debug helper renders the current phase name.

Framing relies on a length field inside each packet header and a type threshold distinguishing headers from payload. Completeness requires both header and full declared length present. After consuming leading bytes, any trailing incomplete fragment is shifted to the start and the end marker is advanced accordingly.

Diagnostic emission has two builds: one forwarding packet and byte dumps to logging helpers, one compiling them away. When enabled, the helpers log header fields and then both hexadecimal and printable renderings of the bytes.

Control packets distinguish modem updates, peer restart announcements and unknown verbs. A modem update that clears carrier drops the stored carrier indication and, when a terminal is attached and not in local ignore mode, hangs up that terminal. A restart announcement requests re-handshake unless already closed. Unknown verbs warn and dump.

Version negotiation moves from awaiting answer to awaiting inquiry upon any answer, then answers an inquiry with a version reply carrying an incremented sequence and next expected sequence before marking established. Modem discovery moves to awaiting modem status, emits a status inquiry with incremented sequence, then on answer reconstructs modem bits from device flags before marking established. Unexpected answers or inquiries in other phases log and dump. A modem wait failure reports an error while still marking established to avoid deadlock.

Inbound data payloads with zero length produce no terminal push. Nonempty payloads deliver up to a fixed cap immediately through per-character insertion with optional attention escape handling, stashing any excess in a surplus area for later. The later delivery helper emits the stashed surplus and clears its count.

Reception reads a bounded chunk from the hypervisor into free reassembly space, then walks complete packets in order, skipping non-header bytes with an error until a header reappears. Data packets are accepted only when usable, control and inquiry packets dispatch to their handlers, unknown types warn and dump, and a requested re-handshake aborts the walk. Remaining bytes are compacted and a single terminal push follows if any data arrived. Interrupt context loops this walk under the port guard until no more bytes arrive, schedules handshake work outside the guard, then opportunistically flushes surplus when a terminal remains and input is not throttled. Phase waiting either polls via synthetic interrupts with millisecond pauses or sleeps on the phase queue, both bounded by the same timeout.

Each port has its own guard protecting phase, reassembly pointers, surplus counts, modem bits and handshake requests. Packet walks, phase changes and surplus flush decisions hold this guard with interrupt preservation, while handshake scheduling and sleeping phase waits occur outside it. Phase notification wakes all waiters.

A write racing teardown observes idle usage and fails rather than touching freed linkage. Truncation of oversized requests is logged. Negative usage reveals caller imbalance. Hangup intentionally discards staged and buffered bytes, which callers must not assume survive.

Malformed framing is contained by skipping to the next header rather than dropping the whole reassembly area. Oversized data bursts are split so terminal input limits are respected. Unexpected control verbs, answers or inquiries never change phase and only warn with a dump. Carrier loss without local ignore terminates the session, and peer restart forces fresh negotiation.
The interrupt handler is the inbound entry for hypervisor data availability, draining all pending bytes and reporting handled in all cases.
